props.title: Burning the Future
props.initialSlug: Coal mining's devastating toll on Appalachia

sections.content: **Burning the Future** (2008) stands as a pivotal environmental documentary that exposed the devastating impact of mountaintop removal coal mining in Appalachia. Director David Novack's unflinching lens follows West Virginia communities fighting against powerful coal companies, similar to the approach taken in **Harlan County, USA** (1976). The film shares thematic DNA with other hard-hitting environmental docs like Gasland (2010) and The Last Mountain (2011), but distinguishes itself through intimate portraits of local activists and stark imagery of destroyed mountain landscapes.

sections.content: The documentary tradition of exposing environmental exploitation gained momentum with The Cove (2009) and **Chasing Coral** (2017), both following **Burning the Future**'s template of combining scientific evidence with emotional storytelling. Novack's work particularly resonates with Dark Waters (2019), which dramatized another West Virginia environmental crisis, showing how documentary investigations often pave the way for dramatic adaptations.

The film's exploration of corporate power versus community resistance echoes through later works like **Dear President Obama** (2016) and **How to Let Go of the World and Love All the Things Climate Can't Change** (2016). These films build on **Burning the Future**'s groundwork, demonstrating how environmental documentaries evolved from simple issue films to complex examinations of social justice, economic inequality, and political power. sections.content: **Burning the Future** helped establish a template for environmental activism documentaries that influenced works like **If a Tree Falls** (2011) and **This Changes Everything** (2015). Its focus on individual stories within larger environmental battles became a crucial storytelling approach, later seen in **Fire in Paradise** (2019) and **Anthropocene: The Human Epoch** (2018).
